sources.title: Dash Academy curriculum — modules 3–19 manifest rows

claims.text: Dash Platform is a layer-2 data-storage and application layer on top of Dash: developers define JSON-Schema data contracts (declarative schemas) and submit signed state transitions, rather than deploying arbitrary user-written code on-chain.

Platform's two core components are Drive (decentralized storage hosted by the masternode network) and DAPI (a decentralized API exposing JSON-RPC and gRPC endpoints through which applications send and retrieve data).

A data contract is a registered schema that declares the document types an application may store, including their fields, types, and indexes — described by upstream as analogous to creating a schema for a document-oriented database such as MongoDB — and every data write is validated against it.

Application data is stored as documents — JSON records in document collections that must conform to the contract's schema — each carrying base fields such as $id, $type, $ownerId, and a $revision that increments on change.
Documents are owned by a Platform identity, and changes are expressed as signed state transitions, so only the owning identity can author changes to its records.

Concrete things built on Platform include DPNS usernames (.dash names tied to an identity), fungible tokens declared inside a data contract rather than written as a smart contract, and NFTs implemented as uniquely-identified document records with built-in transfer and set-price purchase.

The first two data contracts on Dash Platform are DashPay (the social, username-based wallet) and DPNS (the name service that supplies usernames), which together demonstrate the storage-and-schema model in production use.

Working end-to-end example apps exist in the official tutorials — DashMint Lab, an NFT marketplace exercising mint, transfer, price, purchase, and burn; and Dashnote, a notes app demonstrating the document CRUD lifecycle.

Platform query responses can carry cryptographic proofs, so a client verifies an answer against committed state instead of trusting the node that served it — the difference between a decentralized backend and a hosted one.

Drive stores the current state of each application data item on the masternode network rather than on the layer-1 chain (which is expensive for data), and GroveDB provides the authenticated storage that lets those queries return with proofs.

What the reader will build across this course follows the real build order: connect the SDK to testnet, create an identity, register a username, design and publish a data contract, then submit, query, transfer, and purchase documents, and finally declare and operate a token — the path from install to a working decentralized application.

uncertainties.topic: Where the boundary between this lesson and module 4 (why-build-on-dash) should sit, since both name tokens, usernames, and NFTs
uncertainties.resolution: Buildable items (usernames, tokens, NFTs) appear only as short illustrations of the storage model, one or two sentences each; fit-vs-non-fit judgment, the VM roadmap, and the Dash-vs-Credits detail are deferred to module 4.

uncertainties.topic: How much identity/fee detail is needed to explain storage without pulling in module 7 (identities) and module 8 (wallets/keys)
uncertainties.resolution: Name the effect only: data is owned by an identity and changed by signed operations; credit balances and fee mechanics are deferred to module 7.

uncertainties.topic: Whether to state that Dash has no general-purpose smart-contract VM today, or leave that to module 4
uncertainties.resolution: The lesson keeps the declarative-schema-versus-code contrast as the explanation of storage and does not foreground the VM roadmap or timing.
